title: The Fold Line
protagonist: Priya Nakamura, cutting-room lead at a small-batch garment manufacturer
primary_metric: Total dollars (fabric cost plus cutting/marking labor) per finished bodice front panel

options.A: The Fold Cut -- one tracing and one cutting pass per panel, locked to the fabric's true fold
options.B: The Open Cut -- trace and cut two separate mirror-image half-pieces per panel, then nest them edge-to-edge

deliverables.text: A coordinate-grid diagram of the bodice front half-pattern for each cutting method, using reflection across the y-axis to construct the full symmetric panel and labeling the line of symmetry.
A congruence check verifying the original half-pattern and its mirror image are congruent, for each diagram in D1.

A cutting-dimensions and yardage worksheet: total cutting width/length via mixed-number addition of the finished dimensions and allowances, then inches-to-yards conversion by multiplying by the fraction 1/36.

A cost-per-panel table and daily-run projection for each option: fabric cost (yardage adjusted for marker efficiency, times price per yard) plus labor cost (minutes converted to hours, times hourly wage), then multiplied across the shop's 300-panel day.

appendices.title: The Bodice Front Panel: Finished Dimensions

balance.argument_a: The Fold Cut wins on total dollars per panel ($0.9187 vs. $1.0758, a 17.1% gap) because the labor-time gap (0.8 min vs. 1.6 min per panel, at $17.61/hr) is larger in dollar terms than the fabric-efficiency gap (78% vs. 88%) at this fabric's price ($3.70/yd). Scaled to the shop's 300-panel day, Fold Cut saves about $47 a day -- real money against a thin shop margin.
balance.argument_b: The Open Cut uses meaningfully less fabric per panel (0.1638 yd vs. 0.1848 yd, roughly 11% less) because it is not locked to the fold and can nest its two mirror pieces tightly. If fabric prices rise, or if the shop's cutters get faster at the second tracing pass (MA2 is the case's own stated soft spot), the Open Cut's fabric savings can close or overtake the labor gap -- it is the more fabric-efficient method by design, and fabric-price volatility is a real, live risk a fixed labor-cost comparison doesn't fully capture.
balance.margin_basis: Total dollars per panel = fabric cost (cutting-bounding-box area / marker efficiency, converted bolt-inches to yards, times price per yard) + labor cost (marking/cutting minutes converted to hours, times hourly wage). Fold Cut total $0.9187/panel; Open Cut total $1.0758/panel; margin = 100*(1.0758-0.9187)/0.9187 = 17.1%, Fold Cut (A) wins.

modeling_assumptions.text: Bodice front panel finished width 8 3/8 in, length 23 1/4 in, waist hem allowance 1 1/2 in.
Marking + cutting time per panel: Fold Cut 0.8 min, Open Cut 1.6 min (fixed 2:1 ratio).
Marker efficiency point-values: Fold Cut 78%, Open Cut 88% (each a chosen point inside a cited real range).

sensitivity_note: Corrected after running case-readiness's own P5 mechanical sweep (2026-09-18): within EITHER cited real range (Fold Cut 75-82%, Open Cut 82-90%, source S6), the margin narrows or widens but never flips -- e.g. Fold Cut efficiency at the bottom of its real range (75%) still leaves Fold Cut winning by ~13.7%. The verdict only flips under the probe's synthetic +/-50% mechanical stress test, which pushes eff_fold to an unrealistic 39% or eff_open to an unrealistic 132% (both far outside any cited real range) -- see sensitivity_disclosure[] below. MA2 (the labor-time ratio) changes the margin's SIZE substantially but does not flip the winner even at +/-50%. The single most dilemma-relevant real-world risk is therefore the fabric-price twist (see FACILITATOR.md's Twist section and case.json.derived_twist), not either efficiency assumption in isolation.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public source measures marker efficiency for this exact panel shape and 44in bolt width; 78% is a good-faith point chosen from a real cited range (75-82%, source S6) for position-locked/single-piece markers. The case-readiness P5 mechanical sweep flips the verdict only at an unrealistic -50% flex (39%), far outside the cited range; within the real range the verdict does not flip (see sensitivity_note).

No public source measures marker efficiency for this exact panel shape and 44in bolt width; 88% is a good-faith point chosen from a real cited range (82-90%, source S6) for nested/optimized markers. The case-readiness P5 mechanical sweep flips the verdict only at an unrealistic +50% flex (132%, impossible since efficiency cannot exceed 100%), far outside the cited range; within the real range the verdict does not flip (see sensitivity_note).

derived_twist.note: Recomputed by sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist(); winner (A) is unchanged from the base case, margin collapses from 17.1% to ~6.8%. breakeven_price_per_yd solves Total_A(p) = Total_B(p) for the fabric price at which the two options tie.

facilitator.twist_summary: A fabric-price increase is announced mid-discussion (see FACILITATOR.md).

catalog.ask: Priya can cut a garment panel on the fold (trace half, reflect it across a line of symmetry) or open (cut two separate mirror-image pieces and nest them on the bolt). One saves fabric. The other saves labor. Which one actually costs less per panel?
